Verified existing at pubs.opengroup.org; full text now behind free Open Group registration.","url":"https://pubs.opengroup.org/architecture/togaf9-doc/arch/chap20.html","what_it_defines":"The canonical published template for stating a principle: Name (clear, precise, memorable, not implementation-specific), Statement (succinctly and unambiguously communicates the fundamental rule, generally one sentence), Rationale (business benefits, in business language; why the principle matters), Implications (requirements and impacts of carrying out the principle — resources, activities, changed behavior — i.e., the resulting actions). The Implications element satisfies the shop's requirement that definitions carry resulting actions; the 5 criteria seed the review rubric almost verbatim (Robust = decision-guiding, Consistent = mechanical cross-check candidate). RFC 8174 restricts normative force to ALL-CAPS instances only — lowercase 'must'/'should' revert to plain English. Rumelt, \"Good Strategy Bad Strategy: The Difference and Why It Matters\", Crown Business, 2011. Verified via multiple independent summaries and the author's public materials.","url":"https://www.alexmurrell.co.uk/summaries/richard-rumelt-good-strategy-bad-strategy","what_it_defines":"The kernel of good strategy: Diagnosis (what is actually going on; the critical obstacle), Guiding Policy (an overall approach that — like highway guardrails — \"directs and constrains action without fully defining it\"), Coherent Actions (feasible coordinated commitments carrying out the policy). RECOMMENDATION: adapt as the core of the SMALL qualitative fitness-test set for LLM-generated principles and guidelines: tests 2, 3, and 4 are directly executable by a reviewing agent against a draft principle (construct an option the principle rejects; state the reversed principle and check it is coherent; identify the evidence line). Complements TOGAF's five set-level criteria with statement-level teeth.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"Even/Over statements (X even over Y trade-off pairs)","tradition":"Organizational design / strategy practice (The Ready)","source_type":"practice","citation":"Aaron Dignan, \"Brave New Work: Are You Ready to Reinvent Your Organization?\", Portfolio/Penguin, 2019; Jurriaan Kamer, \"Even/Over Statements: The Prioritization Tool That Brings Your Strategy to Life\", The Ready (Medium). RECOMMENDATION: adapt — take the value-pair grammar (already carried into the seed layer via even/over) and the explicit right-side-still-has-value qualifier, which prevents LLM agents from reading a trade-off principle as license to zero out the right side. Do not adopt its content or its manifesto register; cite it as the lineage anchor for the pair form.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"W3C TAG Web Platform Design Principles (named-imperative-principle form)","tradition":"Web standards governance (W3C Technical Architecture Group)","source_type":"standard","citation":"W3C Technical Architecture Group, \"Web Platform Design Principles\", W3C Group Note track (living Editor's Draft, updated June 2026), eds. incl. M. Thomson, J. Yasskin; maintained at github.com/w3ctag/design-principles. Verified at w3ctag.github.io.","url":"https://w3ctag.github.io/design-principles/","what_it_defines":"A maintained catalog of design principles used in actual spec reviews. Each principle: short imperative title, often with a parenthetical canonical name (\"Put user needs first (Priority of Constituencies)\"), followed by explanatory prose and concrete examples of application. The document is versioned, publicly issue-tracked, and applied by the TAG when reviewing proposed web APIs — principles as a working review instrument, not decoration.","form_elements":["Imperative-mood title (a command, not a noun)","Parenthetical stable name for cross-reference","Explanatory prose giving scope and rationale","Worked examples per principle","Living-document governance: public repo, issues, revisions","Principles explicitly consumed by a review process"],"fit_notes":"DESCRIPTION: strongest extant example of principles operated as review infrastructure by a standards body — the exact use the shop intends (rubrics derived from principle definitions, applied by reviewing agents). RECOMMENDATION: adapt the format pattern (imperative title + named handle + prose + examples) as house style for principle Name/Statement rendering, and imitate the governance loop (principles versioned in-repo, cited by ID in reviews). The parenthetical-name convention gives LLM agents a stable citation token. Content is web-specific; only the form and operating model transfer.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"GOV.UK Government Design Principles","tradition":"Public-sector digital service design (UK Government Digital Service)","source_type":"practice","citation":"Government Digital Service / Central Digital and Data Office, \"Government Design Principles\", gov.uk, first published 3 April 2012, last updated 2 April 2025. Verified at gov.uk.","url":"https://www.gov.uk/guidance/government-design-principles","what_it_defines":"A numbered set of short imperative principles (\"Start with user needs\", \"Do the hard work to make it simple\", \"Make things open: it makes things better\"), each followed by explanatory paragraphs and links to posts showing application; maintained and amended over 13 years (a principle was added in 2025), demonstrating the amend-in-place lifecycle TOGAF's Stable criterion describes.","form_elements":["Numbered list, ~10 items","Imperative short title","Explanatory paragraphs with rationale","Links to worked applications","Documented publication/update history"],"fit_notes":"DESCRIPTION: widely imitated exemplar of institutional principles with a public revision history; useful as an existence proof that principle sets stay small (order of ten, matching TOGAF's guidance that too many principles dilute) and evolve under explicit change control. RECOMMENDATION: context-only — it adds no structural element beyond what TOGAF and the W3C TAG form already provide; cite it as calibration for set size, tone, and lifecycle rather than adopting its format.","adopt_potential":"context-only"},{"name":"Lencioni values taxonomy (core / aspirational / permission-to-play / accidental)","tradition":"Management literature (Harvard Business Review)","source_type":"paper","citation":"P. M. Lencioni, \"Make Your Values Mean Something\", Harvard Business Review 80(7), pp. 113–117, July 2002. Verified at hbr.org and via multiple indexes.","url":"https://hbr.org/2002/07/make-your-values-mean-something","what_it_defines":"A classification for value/principle statements: core (genuinely distinctive, guide action, worth bearing cost for), aspirational (needed for the future but not yet true — dangerous if mislabeled core), permission-to-play (minimum table stakes like 'integrity' that distinguish nothing), accidental (emergent traits mistaken for commitments). Famous negative exhibit: Enron's stated values (Communication, Respect, Integrity, Excellence).","form_elements":["Four-way label applied to each candidate value/principle","Test: does it distinguish us and constrain us at real cost?","Anti-pattern: permission-to-play items dressed as principles","Anti-pattern: aspirations asserted as current truth"],"fit_notes":"DESCRIPTION: primary-source management literature giving vocabulary for a specific failure mode — generic virtue-statements posing as principles — that LLM generators are especially prone to producing. - agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- bring-up-bc: Launch an already-scaffolded Bounded Context as a running, online container and verify it reaches the online state
- company-research: Build a cited, bounded intelligence brief on a competitor, peer product, or alternative framework — strategy, product philosophy, recent moves — to ground a brief/PDR in external reality instead of intuition. Use for the consumer-product competitive/market input to problem discovery, or to study a competing framework.
- create-bc: Create a new Bounded Context from scratch — scaffold, remote, manifest registration, and brokered launch — as the lead shop
- derisk-measurement-advisor: Scan a shaping candidate for risk across 10 dimensions — 4 internal (Desirability, Usability, Feasibility, Viability) and 6 external (PESTEL) — and triage each into act-now or track, so the candidate's rabbit-holes and risks name what to test before committing. Reach for it when a bet feels roadmap-ready and you want a structured "what could go wrong, internally and externally?"
- discovery-dialogue: Run the open, interactive discovery conversation that turns a directional or ambiguous prompt into a written, grounded intent record
- discovery-interview-prep: Design a customer discovery interview plan — research goal, target segment, access constraints, and a bias-resistant question set — so a discovery-dialogue turn produces real learning instead of confirmation. Use when the intent record rests on an assumed job that needs to be heard from a real user.
- discovery-process: The end-to-end discovery arc — frame, plan, research, synthesize, validate, decide — used to sequence a multi-turn discovery-dialogue and know which technique skill comes next. Use when a discovery is large enough to need staging rather than a single lens.
- eol-message: Empathetic end-of-life announcement for a retiring product or capability — acknowledges disruption, explains the change as progress, and gives a concrete migration path. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session, and specifically when a brief flips to status:retired.
- incoming-request-advisor: Decode an incoming request before responding — separate the literal ask from the job-behind-it, read the sender's power and stake, and surface hidden assumptions — so a request is classified by its real outcome, not its surface wording. Use at PM-mode entry, at the router's classification boundary, to decide whether a request needs a discovery-dialogue at all.
- jobs-to-be-done: Uncover the stable job a user is hiring the product to do — functional, social, emotional — plus their pains and gains, so intent anchors on a validated job instead of a feature request. Use during the discovery-dialogue when a request smells solution-shaped ("add X").
- opportunity-solution-tree: Move from a target outcome down through opportunities (problems) to candidate solutions to a chosen bet, so shaping commits the candidate to the right problem before it converges on a sketch. Reach for it when a request arrives outcome-shaped or solution-shaped and you need to keep "what are we moving?" upstream of "what do we build?"
- option-tradeoff: Frame two or more shaped options against each other, surface the tradeoffs, and run the deciding conversation with the product authority
- pol-probe: Design a Proof-of-Life probe — a lightweight, disposable experiment that tests one falsifiable hypothesis before expensive work — and land it in the candidate's evidence/experiments line. Reach for it when a shape rests on an assumption cheap enough to test in hours or days and honest enough to kill the bet if it fails.
- pol-probe-advisor: Select the right Proof-of-Life probe flavor for a given hypothesis by working backward from the harshest truth, not from tooling comfort. Reach for it inside shaping when you know an assumption needs testing but aren't sure whether it's a feasibility check, a task test, a narrative, a simulation, or a vibe-coded probe.
- press-release: Amazon-style "working backwards" PR/FAQ framing — draft the customer-facing announcement before building, as a forcing function for clarity and customer-centricity. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session to test whether a direction is genuinely compelling from the outside.
- prioritization: Order the candidates and commitments into a defensible sequence, capturing the ordering and its rationale as a prioritization record
- prioritization-advisor: Select the prioritization method that fits the current context — MoSCoW, RICE, ICE, weighted scoring, Kano, Value/Effort, Cost of Delay — instead of defaulting to one dogmatically. Reach for it inside a prioritization session before scoring anything, to pick the right lens for the stage, data, and decision at hand.
- problem-framing-canvas: Reframe a messy or solution-shaped request into a clear, bias-checked problem statement and a "How Might We" question before committing intent. Use inside the discovery-dialogue when you suspect you're about to solve the wrong problem.
- problem-space-mapping: Continuously maintain the map of the product's problem space so every candidate and intent has a place to hang, producing problem-space map revisions
- problem-statement: Turn a request or a raw job into a crisp, user-centered problem statement using the "I am / trying to / but / because / which makes me feel" frame, so intent names a person and a barrier, not a solution. Use inside the discovery-dialogue to fix the problem before any solutioning.
- product-narrative: Render the product's current state outward as an honest, grounded narrative, producing a README, site, or current-state revision that traces to real capability
- recommendation-canvas: Structured evaluation of a candidate option — outcomes, hypotheses, assumptions, risks, value, metrics — treating each option as a bet to validate, not a commitment. Reach for it inside an option-tradeoff session to turn a raw option list into a defensible pick with rationale.
- reconcile-and-close: Reconcile a completed BC dispatch by consuming its work_done outbox row and closing the corresponding bead as one atomic reconcile-and-close action via the reconcile-and-close executable wrapper
- shaping: Take a validated intent and drive a single candidate to shaped — bounded, de-risked, and ready for a commitment decision
- stakeholder-engagement-advisor: Plan engagement for one specific stakeholder — diagnose their profile and power/impact position, then tailor message, medium, cadence, and a named next action, planning both sides of the relationship. ## Five Criteria for Good Architecture Principles

**Understandable**: the underlying tenets can be quickly grasped and understood by individuals throughout the organization. The intention of the principle is clear and unambiguous, so that violations, whether intentional or not, are minimized.

**Robust**: enable good quality decisions about architectures and plans to be made, and enforceable policies and standards to be created. Each principle should be sufficiently definitive and precise to support consistent decision-making in complex, potentially controversial situations.

**Complete**: every potentially important principle governing the management of information and technology for the organization is defined - the principles cover every situation perceived.

**Consistent**: strict adherence to one principle may require a loose interpretation of another principle. The set of principles must be expressed in a way that allows a balance of interpretations.

**Stable**: principles should be enduring, yet able to accommodate changes. An amendment process should be established for adding, removing, or altering principles after they are ratified initially.

## Documentation Structure

Each principle should have associated rationale and implications statements, both to promote understanding and acceptance of the principles themselves, and to support the use of the principles in explaining and justifying why specific decisions are made.

Yes, this page extensively describes Y-statements as a template for architectural decision records.

## The Template

The template follows this structure:

"In the context of the Web shop service, facing the need to keep user session data consistent and current across shop instances, we decided for the Database Session State Pattern and neglected Client Session State or Server Session State to achieve cloud elasticity, accepting that a session database needs to be designed, implemented, and replicated."

The six components are:
1. **Context**: functional requirement or architecture component
2. **Facing**: non-functional requirement or desired quality
3. **We decided for**: the chosen decision outcome
4. **And neglected**: alternatives not selected
5. **To achieve**: benefits realized
6. **Accepting that**: drawbacks and consequences

## Inventor and Publication

Olaf Zimmermann created Y-statements. He developed them during consulting work when project sponsors wanted decisions "fit each decision on one presentation slide." The approach was presented at SATURN 2012 in a talk titled "Making Architectural Knowledge Sustainable: Industrial Practice Report and Outlook" and subsequently published in an IEEE Software/InfoQ article. The template name derives from its visual resemblance to the letter "Y" and pronunciation similarity to "why."

# RFC 8174 Analysis

Yes, this is RFC 8174 by B. Leiba from May 2017, categorized as BCP (Best Current Practice) 14.

## Key Points

**Capitalization requirement:** The document clarifies that special meanings apply only to uppercase usage. As stated: "The words have the meanings specified herein only when they are in all capitals."

When not capitalized, the document specifies: "When these words are not capitalized, they have their normal English meanings and are not affected by this document."

**Updated boilerplate text:** RFC 8174 provides revised language for document authors. The new recommended phrase includes:

"The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here."

This updates the original RFC 2119 guidance by explicitly restricting the special meanings to all-caps usage, resolving ambiguity about lowercase variants.

## The Strategy Kernel

A good strategy has a logical structure called the kernel, which contains three essential elements: a diagnosis, a guiding policy, and a set of coherent actions.

### The Three Elements:

**1. Diagnosis**
A great deal of strategy work is trying to figure out what is going on—not just deciding what to do, but the more fundamental task of comprehending the situation and identifying the biggest barriers to forward progress. The diagnosis simplifies complexity by identifying certain aspects as critical and others as secondary.

**2. Guiding Policy**
The guiding policy outlines an overall approach to overcoming the obstacles highlighted in the diagnosis. Like the guardrails on a highway, the guiding policy directs and constrains action without fully defining it.

**3. Coherent Actions**
Coherent actions are feasible coordinated policies, resource commitments, and actions designed to carry out the guiding policy.

## Hallmarks of Bad Strategy

Rumelt's four hallmarks of bad strategy are: fluff, failure to face the challenge, mistaking goals for strategy, and bad objectives. More specifically, the most common cause of bad strategy is a weak diagnosis, and the second most common is confusing goals with strategy.

## The Four Types of Values

The article identifies four different types of values: core, aspirational, permission-to-play, and accidental.

**Core Values:** These are values that guide all of your actions and truly make you an individual. Core values serve as the guiding principles and should have an influence on the organization's principles.

**Aspirational Values:** These are values that you aspire to have and are working towards but do not yet have in place.

**Permission-to-Play Values:** These behavioral values are referred to as permission-to-play values by Lencioni and are characterized by normative rules and standards.

**Accidental Values:** These values are determined by the people you may be with or aspire to be like, and they aren't cultivated or even recognized. Accidental values reflect employee interests but have little to do with the organization's actual aim, strategy and basis for success.

## Main Argument

Lencioni argues that most values statements are bland, toothless, or just plain dishonest, and far from being harmless, they're often highly destructive, creating cynical and dispirited employees and undermining managerial credibility.

# ISO/IEC Directives Part 2 - Clause 7 Analysis

## 1) Use of "must"

**"Must" is prohibited as an alternative to "shall".** The document states:

> "Do not use 'must' as an alternative for 'shall'. This avoids confusion between the requirements of a document and external constraints."

"Must" is reserved exclusively for external constraints (laws of nature, legal conditions) that exist outside the document's provisions.

## 2) "Can" vs. "May"

**Yes, "can" shall not replace "may" for permission.** The directive specifies:

> "Do not use 'can' instead of 'may' in this context. 'May' signifies permission expressed by the document, whereas 'can' refers to the ability of a user."

"Can" indicates possibility/capability; "may" indicates permission granted by the document.

## 3) Objective Verifiability

**Requirements must be objectively verifiable.** Clause 5.5 states:

> "Requirements shall be objectively verifiable. Only those requirements that can be verified shall be included."

Subjective phrases like "sufficiently strong" are explicitly prohibited.

## 4) Comprehensibility Standard

**Documents must be understandable to qualified non-participants.** Clause 4 requires documents to:

> "be comprehensible to qualified people who have not participated in their preparation"
